verses.text: I command you therefore before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead at his appearing and his Kingdom:
preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort, with all patience and teaching.
For the time will come when they will not listen to the sound doctrine, but, having itching ears, will heap up for themselves teachers after their own lusts;
and will turn away their ears from the truth, and turn aside to fables.
But you be sober in all things, suffer hardship, do the work of an evangelist, and fulfill your ministry.
For I am already being offered, and the time of my departure has come.
I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith.

From now on, there is stored up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give to me on that day; and not to me only, but also to all those who have loved his appearing.
Be diligent to come to me soon,
for Demas left me, having loved this present world, and went to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia.
Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service.
But I sent Tychicus to Ephesus.
Bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus when you come, and the books, especially the parchments.
Alexander, the coppersmith, did much evil to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds,
of whom you also must beware; for he greatly opposed our words.
At my first defense, no one came to help me, but all left me. May it not be held against them.
But the Lord stood by me, and strengthened me, that through me the message might be fully proclaimed, and that all the Gentiles might hear; and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion.
And the Lord will deliver me from every evil work, and will preserve me for his heavenly Kingdom; to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the house of Onesiphorus.
Erastus remained at Corinth, but I left Trophimus at Miletus sick.
Be diligent to come before winter. Eubulus salutes you, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers.
The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Grace be with you. Amen.

footnotes.content: Paul opens his final charge before *the Judge himself*—Christ at his appearing. When we feel small, remember: the One who knows our heart completely will also vindicate those who have held fast. This weight Paul places on Timothy is not burden alone but assurance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Be urgent in season and out of season"—the preacher's steady heartbeat, not the frantic noise. Reprove, rebuke, exhort: all three flow from patience and teaching, not from anger or haste. A word spoken in love finds soil to grow in, even when it stings.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Itching ears" will always gather false teachers. We hear this warning still: custom-made comfort, doctrine that flatters, spirituality without the cross. Recognize the hunger beneath—people do want truth; they have only been taught that truth should feel good.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The turning away is gradual, one small choice at a time. The ear trained on fables grows deaf to the still, small voice. This is why Paul keeps urging Timothy to hold fast—because the heart's direction is never neutral.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the midst of a wandering age, Timothy is called to sobriety—clear-eyed, steady-footed. Suffering hardship will come. But evangelist's work is not conqueror's work; it is the patient sowing of gospel seed in soil that may or may not yield.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul speaks of his own pouring-out as a libation, a drink offering, final and near. There is no regret in his words, only the quiet peace of a life given wholly. Departure here echoes the Exodus—the Lord's people crossing over at last.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The trilogy of completion: fought, finished, kept. Not "succeeded" or "won all battles," but fought, finished, kept faith. This is the epitaph Jesus would recognize in any life—not perfection, but faithfulness unto the end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The crown of righteousness is stored, not earned—grace upon grace. Notice: "not to me only." Paul will not stand alone. Every soul who has loved his appearing—his return—receives the same crown. We are not islands in hope; we are a beloved company.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Be diligent to come to me soon." In his final days, the apostle asks for companionship. Ministry is not a lonely office; it is lived among the household of faith. Timothy's presence will matter, will comfort, will mean more than the young man may yet know.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Demas loved the present world and left. Yet Crescens and Titus have gone to their work. Not all who walk with Christ will stay until the end. Paul does not rage at Demas; he simply reports the truth. Love does not require blindness to human weakness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Only Luke remains with Paul—the gentle physician and historian. Mark, who once deserted, is now called "useful." Redemption moves quietly through these names: failure is not final, and the Lord restores the fallen to the work they thought was lost forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tychicus sent to Ephesus—the faithful one who carries Paul's words. In isolation, we are never alone if the household of faith moves between us. One sent carries the love of the imprisoned to the free.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A cloak left at Troas, books, parchments—such tender, human detail. Paul needs warmth, needs to read, needs the work of his own hands and mind. The apostle who writes scripture does not despise provision or comfort, and neither should we.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Alexander, the coppersmith, did much evil. Paul does not seek vengeance; he leaves Alexander to the Lord's justice. "The Lord will repay him according to his deeds"—spoken not in bitterness but in the deep conviction that God sees what we cannot.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Timothy must be watchful of Alexander, who greatly opposed their words. Discernment is love's companion—it is not unkind to name who resists truth, and to warn those you cherish to walk carefully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At his trial, all abandoned Paul—the loneliness of standing alone. Yet he speaks grace over them: "May it not be held against them." Here is the heart of the gospel lived out in real sorrow: Paul chooses mercy even over his own betrayal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When all left, the Lord stood by Paul—sustained him, strengthened him. The gospel was fully proclaimed through him, reaching Gentiles. Delivered from the lion's mouth: whether literal beast or metaphor for Rome's might, the Lord's deliverance is sure and real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord will deliver from every evil work and preserve unto his heavenly Kingdom—not ease in this life, but faithfulness unto the Kingdom. Paul's closing doxology rises like incense: "to whom be glory forever and ever." Even in chains, his heart sings.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Prisca and Aquila: tentmakers, teachers, riskers of their lives for Paul. Onesiphorus: whose house sheltered the apostle. These names are the Church—not grand but faithful, tender-hearted, brave in small ways. The Kingdom is built on such kindness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Erastus remains at Corinth; Trophimus lies ill at Miletus. The apostle's powers did not heal every friend. In the shadow of the cross, we learn that faith does not guarantee earthly remedy, only presence, love, and the God who suffers with us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Before winter"—the journey grows cold, time narrows. Those who greet Timothy (Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, Claudia, all the brothers) speak their love across distance. In the last breath of life, we measure love not in grand words but in faithful presence and greeting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Grace be with you." Readers today hear an echo in these closing words: the benediction Paul spoke to Timothy reaches across centuries to us. When we are afraid or alone, that same Lord stands ready to be with *our* spirit, and grace is still enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
